source.title: Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles
source.authors: Nicholas Carlini; Steve Chien; Milad Nasr; Shuang Song; A. Terzis; Florian Tramèr

page_placements.theme: Generalization and privacy leakage require separate measurement

record.tranche_reason: Measures how membership-inference success relates to train-test gap and training choices, but does not measure any listed version's specific outcome.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results on membership-inference success versus model generalization gap and training setup. These are related to the claim's subject but do not measure the behaviors in V1–V8. Its discussion of random-label memorization cites prior work and is not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures membership-inference vulnerability and its relationship to generalization, but its results do not test V1–V8. Width and optimizer comparisons report attack success rather than held-out classification performance. Random-label injections measure privacy scores rather than random-label fitting and generalization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes secondary findings. The central conclusion is that membership-inference attacks should be evaluated by true-positive rates at low false-positive rates, where aggregate accuracy can be misleading. LiRA substantially improves attack success in this regime; generalization gap alone does not determine vulnerability.
record.recipe_differences: Measures membership-inference attack success and its relationship to generalization, rather than the listed interventions and test-error outcomes.
record.method_sensitivity: Membership-inference vulnerability varies with model size and data augmentation; optimizer choice has minimal reported impact. Attack vulnerability can differ substantially at identical train-test gaps.

fits_no_version.finding: Attack vulnerability generally increases with train-test gap, but models with identical gaps can differ by 100-fold in attack vulnerability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization gap is associated with membership-inference vulnerability but does not determine it.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models within the CNN and WRN families are more vulnerable; optimizer choice minimally affects attack success; stronger augmentation reduces vulnerability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Membership-inference vulnerability depends on model size and augmentation, with little optimizer dependence in these experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Section VII-B, Figure 13 reports higher privacy scores for inserted distribution-shifted and randomly labeled examples than for ordinary CIFAR-10 examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Atypical training examples can have more distinguishable membership-dependent loss distributions.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
record.problems: The reported model-gap relationship is shown as a figure without enumerated point values. The paper reports a qualitative trend and large same-gap differences, but gives no uncertainty estimates for these comparisons.

untested.parts: Matched natural-label and random-label training fits and held-out accuracies; random-label privacy scores do not supply these comparisons.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected held-out error and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out error, including training-set size, dropout strength, and joint removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: V1 and V8 originals are cited as background. Neither those citations nor the per-example loss-distribution experiment tests the listed versions. No verdict labels are warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fit and held-out accuracy on natural labels.
Test error as width passes the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected test error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: CIFAR-10 CNN models and Wide ResNets (WRN)
rows.size_stated: CNN models and WRN of various sizes
rows.operation_detail: Compared membership-inference attack TPR at 0.1% FPR with model train-test accuracy gap across training configurations.

conditions.value: CNN models and Wide ResNets of various sizes

rows.measure: Attack TPR at 0.1% FPR versus train-test accuracy gap
rows.value: The text reports an overall trend of greater attack vulnerability with higher train-test gap, and models with identical gaps that were 100× more vulnerable.
rows.note: This measures attack vulnerability, not a property predicting the gap as V7 specifies. Figure 7 values are not enumerated in the text.
rows.check: The reported association and 100-fold differences concern membership-inference vulnerability. No magnitude-aware weight sharpness or other V7 measure is evaluated.

rows.subject: CNN and WRN model families
rows.size_stated: CNN-16, CNN-32, CNN-64 and WRN28 widths 1, 2 and 10
rows.operation_detail: Compared membership-inference attack TPR across target-model architectures.
rows.value: The text reports that larger models are more vulnerable to attacks within both model families.
rows.note: The stated outcome concerns attack vulnerability, not test error or the train-test gap.
rows.check: Larger models have higher attack success rates; this does not establish how test error changes beyond the interpolation threshold.

rows.subject: WRN28-10
rows.operation_detail: Compared membership-inference attack TPR across target-model optimizers.
rows.value: The text states optimizer choice has minimal impact on the attack for both defender and attacker.
rows.note: The outcome is attack performance, not held-out model performance.
rows.check: Change state from absent: negligible optimizer effects on attack success cannot establish absent optimizer effects on held-out classification performance. The comparison varies both target and shadow-model optimizers.

rows.subject: WRN28-10
rows.operation_detail: Compared membership-inference attack TPR across target-model data augmentations.

conditions.value: none, mirroring, mirroring plus shifts, or mirroring plus shifts plus cutout

rows.value: The text reports that stronger augmentation makes models harder to attack because they are less overfit.
rows.note: The paper states the direction qualitatively; the reported measure is attack performance, not the size of the generalization gap.
rows.check: The comparison varies target and shadow-model augmentation and reports attack success. It does not compare dropout or weight-decay removal as V6 requires.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: It discusses generalization and memorization and relates attack success to train–test gaps without testing a listed claim version.

tranche.reason: The study measures membership-inference vulnerability, a different construct from the effects specified in V1–V8.

source_check.notes: Section V-D explicitly reports 100-fold vulnerability differences at identical train–test accuracy gaps. Figure 7 does not enumerate individual plotted values; no magnitude-aware sharpness measure is evaluated.
